newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Focus shifts from aid to economic reform in Bosnia.
newsitem.headline: Focus shifts from aid to economic reform in Bosnia.

text.p: Western donors, shifting their approach to Bosnia, are demanding the new peacetime government adopt a detailed set of economic reforms devised to lay the ground for a self-sustainable economy, experts say.

Economists working for the office of Carl Bildt, High Representative to Bosnia, have proposed an "immediate action agenda" for Bosnia and urged its adoption before an international donors conference set for March in Brussels.

Adopting the proposed set of laws is also a precondition for an agreement with the International Monetary Fund, which donors will be expecting before committing $1.4 billion for Bosnia's reconstruction in 1997, officials said.

The nature of foreign assistance has changed from bringing urgent relief to Bosnia to building a sustainable economy and donors want to see institution-building that would make Bosnia stand on its own feet in a few years' time.

"There must be strong enough prospects that donors' contributions will bring sustained economic recovery, not just temporary relief," David Lipton, assistant secretary at the U.S. treasury told an economic reform conference in Sarajevo.
The IMF and Bildt's office want Bosnia to move quickly to adopt the following laws:

1. Law on a single central bank, which will have the sole authority to issue currency and will operate as a currency board with a fixed exchange rate and full foreign reserve backing for domestic currency.
2. Law on the state budget and for Bosnia's two entities -- Moslem-Croat federation and the Serb republic, based on the principle of no domestic borrowing.
3. Law on external debt, which will ensure debt service on the stock of existing debt and allow acquisition of a new debt.

4. The State tariff law with few exemptions and low tariff rates. The plan recommends improved linkage between two entities' payment systems and reintegration of power, telecommunications systems and railways.

A Bosnian official said the drafts of the laws have been prepared, but several outstanding issues have been forwarded to the three-man collective presidency, the country's top political decision-makers.
But sending every significant issue to the presidency has caused delays in resolving purely technical problems, Bosnia's Minister for Foreign Trade Hasan Muratovic told Reuters on Sunday.

"There is a non-stop improvisation on who needs to decide what and when we can't agree, it all goes to the presidency...We need to be able to reach quick decisions without mulling at a higher level," he said.

Foreign economic experts also proposed a medium-term agenda for Bosnia to be carried out in 1997, which envisages a reform of the banking system, integration of payment systems and promoting private businesses among other measures.
